message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
I've written this as a straightforward, evidence-led case. It uses the strongest controlled study we have, the Varden trial, and the meta-analysis, so the numbers are solid. The arithmetic on output per worker is the key point for the board: because the per-hour gain is larger than the hours cut, every service comes out ahead. I've kept it short and deliberately included the contact centre, because a council-wide policy is simpler and fairer than carving out exceptions.
</author>

<document>
Briefing: Moving All Council Services to a Four-Day Week

1. Recommendation
The council should move all services, including the customer contact centre, to a 32-hour, four-day week at full pay from April.

2. Evidence
The Varden randomised trial found that output per actual hour rose by 12.5% after nine months in case-processing offices, and by 8.5% at 24 months. Actual hours fell by 11%. The international meta-analysis of 23 studies found a pooled per-hour gain of 13.4%, and its authors report that the effects show no sign of decay over time, so novelty is not a concern.

3. Output per worker
Because the per-hour gain (8.5%) is close to the hours cut, and the meta-analysis figure (13.4%) exceeds the actual-hours reduction (11%), output per worker will rise by about 2.4% (13.4% minus 11%).

4. Wellbeing
Sickness absence fell by about a third and resignations roughly halved in the trial offices. These savings come on top of the productivity gain.

5. Contact centre
The contact centre will follow the same model as the other services. Staff will cover the same opening hours on a rota.

6. Conclusion
The evidence supports a council-wide four-day week with no loss of output and substantial wellbeing gains.
</document>
response:
## Verdict

This briefing can't go to the board as written. Its central arithmetic is wrong, and it reverses the trial's clearest finding.

- **Wrong arithmetic:** the output-per-worker calculation is methodologically wrong. Done correctly, output per worker falls.
- **Contradicted by the evidence:** the contact-centre recommendation repeats the arm of the Varden trial that the county had to stop.
- **Misstated figures:** several numbers are wrong or come from studies that can't support them.

Taken together, the conclusion "no loss of output" is contradicted by the evidence the briefing itself cites.

## Problems, most serious first

**1. The contact centre (Sections 1 and 5).** Varden tried this exact model: same staff, a rota, unchanged opening hours.
- Output per employee fell 11.4%.
- In months 10–12, waits were 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices.
- The county ended that arm at month 12. Restoring service would have needed about 12% more staff and raised cost per contact by about 9%.
- The meta-analysis shows the same pattern across seven coverage-bound studies, with output per worker down about 9%. It is the most consistent finding in the literature.

Fairness is a legitimate reason to include the contact centre. But the briefing must then state the cost: either longer waits, or extra staff.

**2. The output-per-worker arithmetic (Section 3).** Three errors:
- **Mixed sources.** The 13.4% comes from the meta-analysis's all-studies pool, which is inflated by uncontrolled designs and scheduled-hours denominators. The 11% comes from Varden. They can't be combined.
- **Wrong operation.** Percentage changes multiply; they don't subtract. Even taking 13.4% at face value: 1.134 × 0.89 = 1.009, so +0.9%, not +2.4%.
- **Wrong per-hour figure.** The figures that fit the 11% hours fall are Varden's own 8.5%, or the meta-analysis's controlled estimate for discretionary work (+9.6%):
  - Varden: 1.085 × 0.89 = 0.966, so **−3.4%** (report's CI −8.0% to +1.2%).
  - Meta-analysis: 1.096 × 0.89 = 0.975, so **−2.5%**.

Your covering note says the per-hour gain is "larger than the hours cut". It isn't: 8.5% is less than 11%. In the trial that measured both, no service came out ahead per worker.

**3. "No sign of decay, so novelty is not a concern" (Section 2).** That meta-analysis claim rested on four long-follow-up studies. All four were uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours, so they can't speak to decay. In Varden, the gain fell from 12.5% to 9.8% on the same timesheet measure. "12.5% then 8.5%" compares two different measures.

**4. Smaller errors.**
- **Sickness absence:** it fell about 27% at 24 months, which is a quarter, not a third.
- **Resignations:** 4.1% against 7.9% is roughly halved, but imprecise.
- **"On top of the productivity gain":** there is no per-worker gain for the savings to sit on top of. Nobody has estimated how far lower sickness and turnover offset the cost.

**5. Scope.**
- **Type of work:** the controlled evidence is for case-processing work in one public employer. "All services" includes other kinds of work the evidence doesn't cover.
- **Size of the cut:** Varden cut hours from 37.5 to 30. Your proposal cuts to 32, and the briefing doesn't give the current baseline, so the size of the cut is unclear.

**6. A missing point that helps you.** About half the gain came from fewer meetings. Cutting meetings is cheap and can be done in any service, including the contact centre, without cutting hours.

## Revised draft

I've rewritten the briefing so it can be defended. Reverse any part you disagree with.

> **Briefing: A Phased Four-Day Week**
>
> **1. Recommendation.** Pilot a 32-hour week at full pay in case-processing and back-office services from April. Keep comparable teams on current hours, and evaluate at 12 months. Run a meeting audit in all services now. Do not move the contact centre without funding about 12% more staff; offer its staff an alternative benefit.
>
> **2. Evidence.** In the Varden randomised trial, case-processing output per actual hour was 8.5% higher than control at 24 months (95% CI 3.4 to 13.8). Actual hours fell 11%, so output per worker was about 3% lower (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). Fewer meetings explained about half the per-hour gain. The gain narrowed from 12.5% to 9.8% between 9 and 24 months.
>
> **3. Contact centre.** The same model, used in Varden's contact centres, cut output per worker by 11%, nearly doubled waiting times, and was stopped at month 12.
>
> **4. Wellbeing.** Sickness absence fell about 27%. Resignations roughly halved, though that estimate is imprecise. The savings are real but have not been quantified.
>
> **5. Cost.** At full pay, cost per case rises about 3%, partly offset by lower absence and turnover.

The meeting audit fits in the "Fair to all staff" position you want to take: every service gets it, regardless of whether it can move to fewer hours.
